unit.title: Perform advanced welding using manual metal arc welding process (MMAW)

summary: This unit takes manual metal arc welding (MMAW) beyond the basics: welding plate and pipe in all positions to a welding procedure specification (WPS), with low-hydrogen and cellulosic electrodes, preheat and controlled distortion. It also covers stainless steel, dissimilar joints, cast iron repairs and hardfacing, and the inspection, testing, repairs, records and team leadership expected of a Level 3 welder.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). You already know how to set up an MMAW machine, strike an arc and run sound fillet welds on the bench. This unit builds on that: **complete joint penetration** butt welds on plate and pipe in every position, welding to a **WPS**, controlling cracking with **preheat** and dry low-hydrogen electrodes, controlling distortion on large work, and welding materials other than mild steel.

At Level 3 you are expected to think like a lead hand. You read the drawing and the WPS, check that the welders are qualified for the work, plan the order of welding, check fit-up and preheat, inspect and test the welds, organise repairs, keep the records and coach the people in your team.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and working welders preparing for structural, plant and pipe work. You should already be able to make sound flat and horizontal fillet welds with E6013 and E7018.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Plan to a procedure
Read drawings and weld symbols, follow the WPS, check welder qualifications and the materials, and plan the welding sequence.
Work safely on advanced and site work
Control the extra hazards of overhead work, heights, confined spaces, stainless fume, wet sites and engine-driven machines.
Choose and look after electrodes and machines
Choose cellulosic, low-hydrogen, iron-powder, stainless, nickel and hardfacing electrodes for the job, keep low-hydrogen electrodes dry, and use the machine's arc controls.
Prepare joints and apply preheat
Bevel, fit up and tack to the WPS, back-gouge where needed, and apply, measure and record preheat and interpass temperature.
Weld plate in all positions
Make multi-run butt and fillet welds in the flat, horizontal, vertical and overhead positions (1G–4G, 1F–4F).
Weld pipe
Make pipe butt welds in the fixed positions (5G, 6G and 2G), from root and hot pass to fill and cap.
Weld special materials
Weld stainless steel, join stainless to carbon steel, repair cast iron and hardface worn parts.
Control distortion
Plan tacking, presetting and balanced sequences so large work stays straight.
Inspect, test, repair and record
Inspect welds with gauges, choose tests, organise repairs to a procedure, keep weld records and coach welders.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on procedures and qualification, drawings, safety, equipment, electrodes, joint preparation, preheat, positional and pipe welding, distortion, defects, inspection, testing and records.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as carbon equivalent, back gouging, stringer, throat, NDT, VRD) and longer answers that explain a method, a procedure or a plan.

**Practical tasks**: vertical-up (3G) and overhead (4G) butt welds on 10 mm plate with bend tests, and a fixed 5G pipe butt weld with a cellulosic root and low-hydrogen fill and cap. You also act as inspector and keep the weld record.

blocks.note: The welding is only half the mark at this level. The assessor also watches your plan, your fit-up and preheat checks, how you clean between runs, and how accurately you inspect and record.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning: drawings, symbols, procedures and qualifications

blocks.p: Structural and plant drawings show welds with the AWS welding symbol. The **reference line** is the horizontal line; the **arrow** points to the joint. A weld symbol **below** the line means the weld is made on the **arrow side** of the joint; **above** the line means the **other side**; on both sides means both.

head: Part of the symbol
What it tells you
rows: Triangle
Fillet weld (the upright leg of the triangle is always drawn on the left)
V, bevel, U or J shape
The groove (butt) preparation
Number to the left of the weld symbol
The weld size, for example the fillet leg length or the groove depth
Numbers to the right
The length of weld, and for intermittent welds the pitch (centre-to-centre spacing), for example 50-150
Circle where the arrow meets the reference line
Weld all round the joint
Flag at that point
Field weld: made on site, not in the shop
Tail (a fork at the end of the line)
Extra information, such as the process, the WPS number or CJP
Contour mark (flat line or curve) with a letter such as G
The shape of the finished face and how to finish it (G = grind)

blocks.p: A **complete joint penetration (CJP)** weld (often called 'full penetration') must fuse through the **whole thickness** of the joint. It is welded from both sides with back gouging, or from one side onto a backing bar or with an open root that the WPS allows. A **partial joint penetration (PJP)** weld fuses only to the depth the drawing gives.

A **WPS** is the written instruction for making a weld so that it will be sound every time. It is backed by a **procedure qualification record (PQR)**: the record of a test weld that was made, tested and passed. A WPS covers a range of conditions; outside that range it does not apply, and another WPS is needed.

head: The WPS states
Examples
rows: Process
MMAW
Base metals and thickness range
Carbon steel group, 6–20 mm
Joint design
Single-V, 60° included angle, 1–2 mm root face, 2–3 mm gap, backing or not, back gouging
Positions
1G, 2G, 3G uphill; 5G uphill
Electrodes
E6010 3.2 mm root; E7018 3.2 and 4.0 mm fill and cap
Current and polarity
DC electrode positive; amps range for each electrode size and run
Preheat and interpass
Minimum preheat 50 °C; maximum interpass 250 °C
Technique
Stringer or weave, maximum weave width, cleaning between runs, travel direction
Heat treatment and testing
Any post-weld heat treatment; the inspection and tests required

blocks.note: If the job needs something the WPS does not cover (another position, a thicker plate, a different electrode), do not stretch the WPS. Stop and ask for one that covers it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A welder proves their skill by passing a **welder qualification test** to the code the Centre uses. The record of it (often called the welder's **ticket** or certificate) lists the process, electrode group, thickness and diameter range and the **positions** the welder may weld. Before giving out the welds on a job, the team leader checks each welder's record against the WPS.

ul: A flat or horizontal test covers only the easier positions; vertical and overhead tests cover more. A **3G and 4G plate pair** is usually taken to cover all positions on plate, and a **6G pipe test** usually covers all positions on plate and pipe, within the code's limits.
Qualifications lapse if they are not used: many codes ask that the welder has used the process within the last six months, or retests. Keep a register with the dates.
Each qualified welder has an **ID number or stamp**, marked next to their welds, so every weld can be traced to the person who made it.

Pipe

blocks.p: Steel for structural or pressure work comes with a **mill certificate** giving its grade, heat number, strength and chemistry. From the chemistry you can work out the **carbon equivalent (CE)**, a single figure for how hardenable, and so how crack-prone, the steel is:

blocks.note: **CE = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15** (each element as a % from the certificate). Example: C 0.18, Mn 1.20, Cr + Mo + V = 0.08, Ni + Cu = 0.25 gives CE = 0.18 + 0.20 + 0.016 + 0.017 = **0.41**.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: As a rough guide, steels with a CE below about 0.40 are easy to weld; between about 0.40 and 0.45 preheat may be needed on thicker joints; above about 0.45 preheat and strict low-hydrogen practice are usually needed. The WPS and the code's tables decide the actual preheat.

flow: Read the drawing, the specification and the weld symbols; list every weld
Find the WPS for each weld and check it covers the material, thickness, position and electrode
Check that each welder is qualified for the welds you give them
Check the materials against the mill certificates, and the electrodes and oven
Plan access, staging, safety controls and permits
Plan the tacking and welding sequence to control distortion
Set the hold points for inspection: fit-up, preheat, root, final visual, NDT
Brief the team, then check and record as the work goes on

sections.title: Safety on advanced and site work

blocks.p: All the hazards of basic MMAW (shock, arc light, fume, fire, burns) still apply. Advanced work adds new ones: welding overhead, at height, inside tanks, on stainless steel, in wet trenches and with engine-driven machines on site.

head: Situation

rows: Overhead and vertical welding

Leather cape or jacket and sleeves, buttoned collar
Flame-resistant skull cap or hood
Ear plugs to stop spatter entering the ears
Position yourself to the side of the falling spatter
Work at height
Falls; falling objects; sparks falling on people and materials below
A proper work platform or scaffold, or fall protection anchored as the site says
Cables secured so their weight cannot pull you
Area below cleared, barriered and watched by a fire watch
Confined spaces (tanks, vessels, pits)
Too little oxygen, toxic or flammable gas, fume build-up, heat, shock, hard rescue
Confined space permit and hot work permit
Space emptied, cleaned and isolated; air tested before and during work
Forced ventilation or extraction, **never oxygen**
Standby person outside, with communication and a rescue plan
Cylinders kept outside
Stainless steel
Fume contains **hexavalent chromium**, which can cause cancer
Extraction at the arc first
Respirator where the risk assessment says
Head kept out of the plume
Wet sites, trenches and steel structures
Electric shock through sweat, water and steel
Machine with a voltage reduction device (VRD)
Dry gloves, insulating mat

Engine-driven welder
Carbon monoxide in exhaust; fuel fire
Set up outdoors, away from doors, windows and air intakes
Refuel with the engine off and cool
Radiographic testing (X-ray or gamma)
Radiation
Only trained, licensed operators; stay outside the barriers and obey the warning signs and lights

flow: Permit to work for the confined space and a hot work permit, signed by the authorised person
Empty, clean and isolate the space from all pipes, power and moving parts
Test the air (oxygen, flammable gas, toxic gas) before entry and keep testing during the work
Set up forced ventilation or fume extraction; keep gas cylinders and the machine outside
Use a VRD machine, dry PPE and an insulating mat; keep leads in good condition
A trained standby person stays at the entrance the whole time, with a way to talk to the welder
Rescue plan and equipment ready before anyone goes in

blocks.note: Never 'freshen' the air in a tank with oxygen. Oxygen-enriched air makes clothing and hair catch fire easily and burn fiercely. Use forced air from a fan or blower.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **VRD** keeps the open-circuit voltage between the electrode and the work at a low, safer level until the electrode touches the work to strike an arc, then lets the full voltage through. It cuts the risk of shock when you change electrodes or brush against the holder in wet or cramped places. Use it on site and in confined spaces, and check it works (many machines have a VRD lamp).

ul: Check permits are in place before work starts, and that the controls on them are really there.
Check the PPE of every welder, especially for overhead and confined-space work.
Plan heat-stress breaks: a welder in leathers in a steel tank or on a roof in the Jamaican sun can overheat in minutes. Water and rest in the shade.
Keep the fire watch going during the work and for the time the permit says afterwards.
Report injuries, near misses and damaged equipment, and tag faulty gear out of use.

sections.title: Machines and electrodes for advanced work

head: Control
What it does
When it helps
rows: Hot start
Gives a short burst of extra current as the arc strikes
Low-hydrogen electrodes that are hard to start; avoids porosity and cold starts
Arc force (dig)
Raises the current when the arc gets very short, so the electrode does not stick
Cellulosic root runs, where a tight, digging arc is needed
Anti-stick
Cuts the current if the electrode sticks, so it does not glow red
Easier freeing of a stuck electrode
VRD
Keeps the open-circuit voltage low until the arc is struck
Wet, cramped and site work
Remote control (hand or foot)
Lets the welder change the current at the joint
Pipe and positional work, where the current must change round the joint and the machine is far away

blocks.p: Most advanced work is done on **DC** from an inverter, rectifier or engine-driven welder: the arc is steadier out of position, and cellulosic E6010 and most stainless and nickel electrodes need DC. AC is used mainly where arc blow is a problem. On long leads, use cable heavy enough for the current: thin, long cables heat up and the voltage drop weakens the arc.

In an AWS code such as E7018: **E** = electrode; **70** = at least 70 000 psi (about 480 MPa) tensile strength; the **third digit** gives the positions (1 = all positions, 2 = flat and horizontal fillets only, 4 = flat, horizontal, overhead and vertical-down, as on E7048); the **last two digits** give the coating and current.

head: Electrode
Coating
Current
Used for
Points to know

Deep, digging, forceful arc

High hydrogen: not for crack-prone steels
**Never bake**: the coating needs its moisture

blocks.p: Some packets carry extra letters: **H4** or **H8** means the weld metal has no more than about 4 or 8 ml of hydrogen per 100 g; **R** means the coating resists moisture pick-up; **-1** (as in E7018-1) means improved toughness.

ul: Store unopened packs in a dry store. Once opened, keep E7018 in a heated **holding oven** (often about 120–150 °C).

Take out only what you will use in a short time, in a heated portable **quiver** on site. Codes limit how long low-hydrogen electrodes may be out of the oven (often about 4 hours, less in very humid air); the WPS or the Centre's rules give the time.

Electrodes left out too long, or found damp, are **re-baked** at the maker's temperature and time (often about 350 °C for 1–2 hours) and only the number of times the maker allows; otherwise scrap them.
Keep an **oven log**: oven temperature checked and recorded at least once a shift, and re-bakes recorded.
Damp low-hydrogen electrodes put hydrogen into the weld: porosity and, in hard steel, **hydrogen cracking**, which can appear hours after welding.

blocks.note: Jamaica's humid air, especially in the rainy seasons and near the sea, puts moisture back into an open box of E7018 within hours. Treat oven discipline as part of the weld, not as housekeeping.
blocks.label: Jamaica

Contains molybdenum like 316, for better resistance to pitting in salt and chemicals
Stainless to carbon or low-alloy steel
E309L

Cast iron repair
Nickel (often called 'nickel 99') or nickel-iron ('nickel 55')
Soft, ductile weld metal that stretches as it cools instead of cracking; nickel-iron is stronger, for thicker or ductile iron
Worn parts

sections.title: Joint preparation, preheat and distortion control

head: Preparation
Typical use
Typical sizes (always use the WPS)
rows: Square edge
Thin plate; or thicker plate welded from both sides with deep penetration
Gap about 0–3 mm
Single-V
Plate about 6–20 mm welded from one side
Included angle about 60°
Root face about 1–2 mm
Root gap about 2–3 mm
Single-V on a backing strip
One-sided CJP welds where the back cannot be reached
Wider gap (often about 5–6 mm) and no root face, so the root fuses into the strip
Double-V
Plate about 20 mm and over, welded from both sides
Less weld metal than a single-V; runs balanced on both sides to cut distortion
Single-U or J
Thick plate
Less weld metal than a V at large thickness; machined or gouged
Pipe bevel
Pipe butt welds
Often 30–37.5° each side (factory bevels are usually 37.5°), root face about 1.5 mm, gap about 2.5–3 mm

ul: Bevel angle, root face and gap to the WPS, measured with a bridge cam gauge or a gap gauge.
Misalignment (**hi-lo**) of the plate or pipe surfaces kept within the WPS limit.
Joint faces and 25 mm either side clean to bright metal: no paint, oil, rust, mill scale or moisture.
Tack welds made by a qualified welder with the WPS electrode and preheat; small but fully fused; ends ground to a **feather edge** so the root run fuses into them without a lump.

blocks.p: On a CJP weld made from both sides, the root of the first side always has some unfused or contaminated metal at its back. Before the second side is welded, that metal is removed by **back gouging**: with **air carbon arc gouging** (a carbon electrode and a jet of compressed air) or with a grinder, down to sound weld metal. The groove is ground smooth and checked (often with dye penetrant or magnetic particles) before welding.
**Hydrogen cracking** (cold cracking) forms in or beside the weld, often in the heat-affected zone, when three things meet:

ul: **Hydrogen** in the weld, from damp flux, rust, oil, paint or moisture on the joint;
a **hard, crack-sensitive** structure, from steel with a high carbon equivalent or thick plate that cools the weld quickly;
**stress**, from shrinkage and from a joint that is tightly held (restraint).

blocks.p: The cracks can appear **hours, even a day or two, after welding**, so a weld that looked good at the end of the shift can crack overnight. Preheat helps because it **slows the cooling**: hydrogen has time to escape, and hard zones are less likely to form.

head: Raises the preheat needed
Lowers it
rows: Higher carbon equivalent
Lower carbon equivalent
Thicker plate, or several thick parts meeting
Thinner plate
High restraint
Free-to-move joints
Higher-hydrogen electrodes or damp electrodes
Dry low-hydrogen electrodes (H4, H8)
Small, fast runs (low heat input)
Larger runs with more heat input, within the WPS

flow: Read the minimum preheat and maximum interpass temperature on the WPS
Heat evenly with a heating torch or electric heating pads, over a band each side of the joint at least as wide as the plate is thick and not less than about 75 mm
Let the heat soak through, then measure on the plate about 75 mm from the joint edge (or where the WPS says), on the side away from the flame where you can
Check again before each run: the joint must be at or above the minimum and below the maximum interpass temperature
Record the readings, times and welder on the weld record

head: Tool
How to use it
rows: Temperature-indicating crayon

Each crayon melts at its rated temperature. Mark the plate: a mark from a crayon rated at the **minimum** must melt (hot enough); a mark from a crayon rated at the **maximum interpass** must **not** melt (not too hot).
Contact thermometer
Probe pressed on the clean plate; gives a reading in °C
Infrared thermometer
Quick, but shiny or scaly surfaces can read wrongly; check it against a contact reading

ul: **Interpass temperature** is the temperature of the joint just before the next run. If it is too low, reheat. If it is above the maximum (often about 250 °C for carbon steel, lower for stainless), stop and let it cool: too much heat spoils the toughness of the weld and heat-affected zone.
Even where no preheat is needed, a damp or dewy joint is warmed until it is dry and warm to the touch before welding. Morning dew and rain are common on Jamaican sites.
Never judge preheat by hand or by colour: steel shows no colour at all until it is several hundred degrees hotter than any normal preheat.

blocks.note: Work out a temperature rise as a simple difference: if the WPS asks for 100 °C and the plate reads 64 °C, it must rise by another 36 °C.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Weld metal shrinks as it cools, and pulls the parts with it. On large work this shows as **angular distortion** (the plates of a V butt close up like a book), **bowing** (a long beam curves along its length), **longitudinal and transverse shrinkage**, and **buckling** of thin plate. The more weld metal and heat, and the further the welds are from the middle of the section, the more it moves.

head: Control
How it works
rows: Do not over-weld
Weld only to the size on the drawing; extra metal means extra shrinkage
Choose the preparation
A double-V needs less weld metal than a single-V and can be balanced on both sides
Presetting
Set the parts at a small angle the opposite way, so the shrinkage pulls them into line
Pre-cambering
Bend a long member slightly the opposite way before welding
Balanced welding
Weld opposite sides in turn, or two welders work opposite each other, so the pulls cancel
Back-step and skip welding
Weld short lengths in a planned order (each one started ahead and welded back to the last, or spread along the joint), so the heat does not build up in one place
From the middle outwards
Lets the shrinkage move freely towards the ends
Restraint (clamps, jigs, strongbacks)
Holds parts in line; but the more a joint is restrained, the more stress is locked in and the higher the risk of cracking, so it must be used with care and with the right preheat

flow: Check the plates are straight and the web square to the flanges; clamp on a flat table or in a jig
Tack at even spacing along both sides of the web, with tacks opposite each other
Weld the four fillets in a balanced order: opposite fillets in turn, from the middle outwards, in back-step or skip lengths
Two welders working opposite each other at the same time is best
Check straightness with a string line and square as the work goes on; change the order if it starts to bow
Measure and record the final straightness; any straightening is done by a competent person to a procedure

blocks.p: Out of position, gravity pulls on the weld pool. The answer is the same in every position: **a smaller pool**, kept under control with the right current, a short arc, the right angle and the right bead pattern.

blocks.note: The current figures are typical. Every WPS gives an amps range for each electrode and run: stay inside it and test on scrap in the same position before welding the job.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A WPS sometimes gives one run's current as a percentage of another's. Work it out by multiplying: a root at 100 A with fill runs 20% higher gives 100 × 1.20 = **120 A**; a flat setting of 130 A reduced by 10% for overhead gives 130 × 0.90 = **117 A**.

ul: Strike, let the pool form, then weave across the joint with a short arc, **pausing at each edge** long enough to fill the toe, and moving quickly across the middle.
Climb steadily: each weave sits just above the last. If the pool bulges or drips, the current or the pause in the middle is too much.
Keep the weave within about 2½ to 3 times the core wire diameter; a wider joint gets two or more side-by-side runs on the cap.

E7018 is welded **uphill**. Vertical-down with most low-hydrogen electrodes leaves lack of fusion and trapped slag, because the fluid slag runs ahead of the arc. Only electrodes made for it (such as E7048) and only where the WPS says.
Full leathers, cap, collar buttoned, ear plugs. Stand to the side so spatter and slag do not fall straight onto you.
Use a smaller electrode and a lower current, hold a **very short arc**, and lay small stringers. A long arc or a large pool drips.
Clean every run completely: overhead beads tend to be convex with slag trapped at the toes; grind high spots before the next run.

flow: Root run: full fusion of both root faces, with even penetration on the back (a small keyhole on an open root)
Clean the root completely; grind the face of the root if it is humped or has slag lines at its edges
Fill runs: each run fused into the side walls and the run below; clean every run
Stagger the stops and starts of each layer, at least about 25 mm apart
Cap: even height and width, overlapping each edge of the groove by about 1.5–2 mm, blended into the plate with no undercut
Back gouge and weld the second side where the WPS asks

ul: Before restarting, chip the crater and grind the end of the stopped run to a **taper**, so the new run fuses into it without a lump or a cold lap.
Strike just ahead of the crater on the weld line, bring the arc back to fill it, then carry on.
Low-hydrogen electrodes can leave porosity at a cold start: strike a little ahead and run back over the start, or use the machine's hot start.

blocks.p: Pipe welding joins the hardest positions in one joint. In the fixed **5G** position (axis horizontal) one weld goes from overhead at the bottom, up the vertical sides, to flat at the top. In **6G** (axis at 45°) the joint also slopes, so every angle changes as you go round. That is why the 6G test is seen as the hardest, and why passing it covers so much.

Positions round a fixed pipe are given like a clock seen from the end: **12 o'clock** is the top, **6 o'clock** the bottom, 3 and 9 o'clock the sides. A run round the whole pipe is about **π × outside diameter** long: a 114 mm pipe needs about 3.14 × 114 = 358 mm of weld per run, and a 219 mm pipe about 688 mm.

flow: Check the WPS: pipe size and wall, bevel, root face, gap, electrodes and current
Bevel the ends (or check factory bevels), and clean to bright metal inside and out for about 25 mm
Set the gap with a spacer (often a piece of filler rod of the right size) and line the pipes up; check hi-lo all round
Tack in three or four places, spread round the pipe, with the WPS electrode; grind each tack's ends to a feather edge
Fix the pipe in the test position at a comfortable height, with the axis level (5G) or at 45° (6G)

head: Point
Uphill (vertical-up)
Downhill (vertical-down)
rows: Where used
Plant, pressure and water pipe; most training tests
Cross-country pipelines
Electrode
E6010 (or as the WPS says), or E7018 for some roots
E6010 cellulosic, made for downhill
Direction
Start just past 6 o'clock and weld up each side to finish just past 12 o'clock
Start at 12 o'clock and weld down each side to 6 o'clock
Fit-up
Gap about 2.5–3 mm; small root face
Smaller gap and root face; higher current; fast travel
Technique
Small, steady **keyhole** at the front of the pool; electrode pushed into the joint

head: Run
Purpose and method
rows: Root
Fuses both root faces and gives an even bead on the inside. Keep the keyhole the same size all round; feed the electrode further into the joint at the bottom.
Hot pass
Laid straight after the root, at a higher current, to fuse it and burn out the slag trapped at its edges ('wagon tracks'); grind the root first if it is humped.
Fill
Fills the groove with E7018 uphill, each run fused and cleaned; stops and starts staggered.
Cap
Even height and width, slightly wider than the groove, with no undercut. On 2G pipe the fill and cap are stringers laid from the bottom up.

head: Where
Fault
Usual cure
rows: Bottom (5 to 7 o'clock, overhead)
**Concavity or suck-back**: the inside of the root is hollow
Very tight arc, push the electrode further into the joint, keep the keyhole small
Top (11 to 1 o'clock, flat)
**Excess penetration**, icicles or burn-through: the pipe is hot and the pool sags inside
Reduce the current slightly (remote control), travel a little faster, angle the electrode back, keep the keyhole small
Sides (vertical)
Lack of fusion at one root face; undercut inside
Aim the arc at both faces; keep the angle square to the pipe
Anywhere
Lack of root penetration
Current too low, gap too small, root face too big, or travel too fast

blocks.p: Pipe that has been lifted with magnets, or long pipelines, can be magnetised, especially near open ends. On DC, the field pushes the arc to one side. Try moving the work clamp, wrapping the work lead round the pipe near the joint, shortening the arc and angling the electrode against the blow, welding towards a heavy tack, and lowering the current. AC reduces arc blow, but only with an electrode that runs on AC (E6011 instead of E6010, for example), and only if the WPS allows the change.

ul: Look at the inside of the root with a torch and an inspection mirror where you can reach, for even penetration with no concavity, burn-through or lack of fusion.
Check the cap for even width and height, undercut, porosity and cracks, and blend at the tie-ins.
On tests, strips are cut from set places round the coupon so the flat, vertical and overhead parts are all bent; production pipe is often radiographed.

sections.title: Stainless steel, dissimilar joints, cast iron and hardfacing

blocks.p: Austenitic stainless steels such as **304** and **316** resist corrosion because of their chromium (and, in 316, molybdenum). Welding can spoil that if the wrong electrode, too much heat or dirt from carbon steel gets in.

ul: Use the matching low-carbon electrode: **E308L** for 304/304L, **E316L** for 316/316L. The L (low carbon) stops chromium being tied up as carbides near the weld.

Stainless conducts heat poorly and expands a lot, so it holds heat and distorts. Use a low current, small **stringer** runs and a short arc; keep the interpass temperature low (often below about 150–175 °C).
Keep stainless apart from carbon steel: **stainless-only** wire brushes, grinding discs and clamps, and benches covered. Carbon steel dust embeds in the surface and rusts, leaving brown spots.

Remove slag and the coloured **heat tint** after welding by the method the Centre allows (stainless brush, abrasive, or pickling paste with full precautions), because heat tint lowers corrosion resistance.
Stainless fume contains **hexavalent chromium**: extraction at the arc, and a respirator if needed.
Stainless is not magnetic, so surface cracks are found with **dye penetrant**, not magnetic particles.

blocks.p: When a mild steel bracket is welded to a stainless tank, the weld metal mixes with some of each. With E308L, the carbon steel dilutes it so much that the weld can become hard and crack. **E309L** has extra chromium and nickel to allow for that mixing. Clean both parts, use the lowest current that fuses well, and keep the heat low so the thin stainless does not warp.

Cast iron has a lot of carbon (often 2–4%), so it is brittle and has almost no stretch. As a weld shrinks, the casting cannot give, and it cracks. Repairs therefore aim to keep the casting from getting hot in one place and to keep the weld soft.

flow: Clean off oil and dirt; find both ends of the crack (dye penetrant helps)
Drill a small **stop hole** (often about 3–6 mm) just beyond each end, so the crack cannot run further
Grind the crack out into a U or V groove, down to sound metal
Warm the casting gently and evenly if the procedure says so
Weld with a **nickel or nickel-iron electrode**, at low current, in **short runs** of about 25–40 mm
**Peen** each run lightly with a round-nosed hammer while it is still hot, to stretch it and relieve the shrinkage stress
Let the area cool until it is just warm to the hand before the next run; spread the runs along the crack
Cool the finished repair slowly (cover it or wrap it), then check again for cracks

blocks.p: **Hardfacing** lays a hard, wear-resistant layer on parts that wear: excavator bucket teeth and edges, crusher parts, conveyor screws, and sugar-mill rollers and knives. Hardfacing in sugar factories during the crop is a familiar job in Jamaica.

ul: Clean the part and grind off cracked or work-hardened metal.
If the part is badly worn, first restore its size with a **build-up** electrode, which is tough, not hard.
On high-carbon steel, lay a **buffer layer** first if the maker says, so the hard layer does not crack off.
Lay the hardfacing in the pattern the job needs (stringers, dots or a waffle pattern) and keep to the number of layers the maker gives (often two or three): more layers are likely to crack or spall.
Some hard deposits form fine cross-cracks as they cool (relief checks). Ask the maker or your instructor whether they are normal for that electrode before rejecting the part.
Manganese steel parts (such as some crusher jaws) must be kept cool while welding; follow the maker's instructions.

sections.title: Inspection, testing, repairs and leading the team

head: Stage
What to check
rows: Before welding
Drawing and WPS; welder qualified; materials and electrodes right; fit-up (angle, root face, gap, hi-lo); cleanliness; preheat
During welding
Current and electrode for each run; interpass temperature; cleaning between runs; root penetration; back gouging
After welding
Size and profile; cap height; undercut depth; porosity; cracks; arc strikes; spatter; distortion; welder's ID marked

blocks.p: Use the right gauges: a **bridge cam gauge** measures cap height, undercut depth, fillet throat, misalignment and preparation angle; fillet gauges measure leg length; a hi-lo gauge measures pipe misalignment; a torch, mirror and magnifier help you see. The limits (for example the greatest cap height, often about 3 mm, and the deepest undercut, often under 1 mm) come from the code and the WPS, not from what looks good.

A weld outside a limit is recorded as **non-conforming** and put right by the method the procedure allows, then checked again: for example, a cap that stands too high is ground down to the limit, and undercut that is too deep is filled with a small run and blended. Extra weld metal on a cap does not make the joint stronger; it adds stress at the toes.

head: Method
Finds
Points to know
rows: Visual (VT)
Surface faults, size and shape
Done on every weld, first
Dye penetrant (PT)
Cracks and pores open to the surface
Any non-porous metal, including stainless and aluminium; quick and cheap; surface must be clean
Magnetic particle (MT)
Cracks at or just below the surface
Magnetic steels only; fast on structural welds and back-gouged grooves
Ultrasonic (UT)
Flaws inside the weld, especially flat ones: lack of fusion, cracks
No radiation; needs a trained operator; good on thick welds
Radiography (RT)
Flaws inside the weld, especially porosity and slag
Gives a film or image record; radiation hazard; on the image, porosity, slag, lack of fusion and cracks show **dark**, excess penetration shows light

head: Test
What it shows
rows: Face, root and side bend tests
Strips are bent round a former; cracks or lack of fusion open up. A root bend stretches the root; side bends are used on thicker plate
Nick-break test
A strip notched at the weld edges is broken through the weld, so the inside of the weld can be seen
Fillet break test
The upright of a tee is hammered over so the fillet breaks and shows its root fusion
Macro-etch
A cut section is ground, polished and etched to show the fusion, the runs and the heat-affected zone
Tensile, impact and hardness
Strength, toughness and hardness, mostly for procedure qualification

ul: The test follows a written procedure: pipe size and wall, bevel and gap, electrodes and current range.
The coupon is marked with the welder's number and fixed at 45°; it must not be turned. The inspector checks the fit-up and watches the welding.
The weld is inspected by eye, then bend strips are cut from set places round the pipe (so overhead, vertical and flat parts are all tested), or the weld is radiographed.
Bend strips must show no open fault bigger than the code allows (often about 3 mm).

head: Fault
Usual causes
Prevention
rows: Lack of side-wall fusion
Current too low; arc not aimed at the side wall; runs placed badly; travel too fast
Correct current; angle the arc into each side; plan run placement
Slag lines and wagon tracks
Slag not cleaned from the toes of the run below; notches between runs
Clean and grind between runs; hot pass after the root
Excess root penetration
Gap too wide; current too high for the root; travel too slow
Correct gap and current; small keyhole
Root concavity
Overhead root on pipe; arc too long; electrode not pushed in
Tight arc; push the electrode into the joint at the bottom
Hydrogen cracking (often in the HAZ, sometimes delayed)
Damp electrodes; dirty joint; no or too little preheat; hard steel; restraint
Dry low-hydrogen electrodes; clean joints; preheat to the WPS
Centreline (solidification) cracking
Deep, narrow runs; high restraint; dirty plate
Runs wider than they are deep; correct current and speed
Start porosity with E7018
Cold start, long arc at the start
Strike ahead and run back; hot start; short arc
Arc strikes
Striking off the joint; holder touching the job
Strike only in the groove; hang the holder up

flow: Mark the extent of the fault (by NDT where needed) and record it
Remove it by grinding or air carbon arc gouging, down to sound metal
Confirm it is all gone with dye penetrant or magnetic particles before welding
Shape the groove with sloping ends so it can be welded and fused
Preheat as the repair procedure says (often higher than for the original weld)
Re-weld to the approved repair procedure, by a qualified welder
Inspect again with the same methods, and record the repair

blocks.note: Never weld over a crack, fill it with body filler, or peen it closed: the crack is still there and will grow. Codes often limit how many times one spot may be repaired.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Record
What it holds
rows: Weld map
The drawing with every weld numbered
Weld log
For each weld: number, WPS, welder ID, electrode type and batch, preheat readings, date, inspection and NDT results, repairs
Welder qualification register
Each welder's tests, the ranges covered and the dates, so qualifications stay current
Electrode oven log
Oven temperatures, re-bakes and batches issued
Non-conformance and repair reports
What was wrong, the cause, the repair and the re-inspection

flow: Look through the inspection results each week for patterns: by welder, by position, by fault
Watch the welder at work without stepping in; check the machine settings and electrodes too
Explain the fault and its cause, and show the right technique (for undercut: shorter arc, correct current, pause at the edges)
Let them practise on scrap in the same position while you watch
Check their next production welds and praise the improvement
If a fault shows across the team, hold a short toolbox talk on it; record the coaching

blocks.note: A welder who is welding without having read the WPS is stopped at once, not at the end of the joint. Go through the WPS together, then check the welds already made against it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can read weld symbols, including size, arrow and other side, all-round, field weld and CJP.
I can explain what a WPS, a PQR and a welder qualification are, and check a welder is qualified for a job.
I can name the AWS positions 1G–6G and 1F–4F.
I can work out a carbon equivalent and say what it means for preheat.
I can control the hazards of overhead work, heights, confined spaces, stainless fume and wet sites.
I can choose E6010, E7018, E7024, E308L, E316L, E309L, nickel and hardfacing electrodes for the right jobs, and keep low-hydrogen electrodes dry.
I can use hot start, arc force, VRD and remote control.
I can prepare, fit up and tack joints to a WPS, and explain back gouging.
I can explain hydrogen cracking and apply, measure and record preheat and interpass temperature.
I can make multi-run butt and fillet welds in the vertical, horizontal and overhead positions.
I can weld a fixed pipe from root and hot pass to cap, and correct root faults round the pipe.
I can weld stainless steel, join stainless to carbon steel, repair cast iron and hardface a worn part.
I can plan tacking and welding sequences to control distortion.
I can inspect welds with gauges and choose NDT and destructive tests.
I can organise a repair to a procedure and keep the weld records.
I can coach a welder whose welds show a repeated fault.

terms: Arc force (dig)
A machine control that raises the current when the arc gets short, so the electrode does not stick
Back gouging
Removing the back of the first side of a weld down to sound metal before welding the second side
Back-step welding
Welding short lengths, each started ahead and welded back towards the last, to spread heat
Carbon equivalent (CE)
A figure worked out from a steel's chemistry to judge how crack-prone it is
Cellulosic electrode
An electrode such as E6010 with a deep, digging arc, used for root runs; never baked
CJP
Complete joint penetration: weld fused through the whole thickness of the joint
Concavity (suck-back)
A root that is hollow on the inside, common at the bottom of a fixed pipe
Field weld
A weld made on site, shown by a flag on the weld symbol
Hardfacing
Laying a hard, wear-resistant deposit on a part
Hi-lo
Misalignment of the surfaces of two plates or pipes at a joint
Hot pass
The run laid straight after the root, at higher current, to fuse it and burn out slag
Hydrogen cracking
Cracking caused by hydrogen, a hard structure and stress; can appear hours after welding
Interpass temperature
The temperature of the joint just before the next run
Keyhole
The small hole at the front of the pool in an open root, showing it is melting through
Low-hydrogen electrode
An electrode such as E7018 whose dry coating puts very little hydrogen into the weld
Mill certificate
The steel maker's record of a batch's grade, heat number, strength and chemistry
NDT
Non-destructive testing: VT, PT, MT, UT, RT
Overlap (cold lap)
Weld metal that has flowed onto the plate beyond the toe without fusing to it
Peening
Lightly hammering a hot weld run to relieve shrinkage stress
PQR
Procedure qualification record: proof that a WPS gives sound welds
Preheat
Heating the joint before welding to slow cooling and prevent cracking
Presetting
Setting parts at an angle before welding so the shrinkage pulls them straight
Stop hole
A small hole drilled at the end of a crack so it cannot run further
Stringer bead
A run laid straight, with little or no side-to-side movement
Ticket
Trade name for a welder's qualification certificate
Throat
The distance from the root of a fillet weld to the middle of its face
VRD
Voltage reduction device: keeps the open-circuit voltage low until the arc is struck
Weld map
A drawing with every weld numbered, used for records and traceability
WPS
Welding procedure specification: the written instructions for making a weld

c1.title: Beam splices for a church hall in Port Maria
c1.text: Garfield leads three welders splicing steel roof beams for a church hall in Port Maria, St Mary. The beams are already lifted into place, so the top flange splice is welded from above, the web is vertical and the bottom flange is welded from below. The flanges are 16 mm thick, joined with CJP single-V butt welds using E7018. The WPS gives a minimum preheat of 50 °C and a maximum interpass temperature of 250 °C. It rained overnight and the steel is wet with dew. One welder, Ricardo, holds a qualification for 1G and 2G plate only.

c2.title: A pipe tie-in at a pumping station in Yallahs
c2.text: Nordia is welding a 114 mm carbon steel water main into a pumping station in Yallahs, St Thomas. The pipe is fixed with its axis horizontal (5G). The WPS gives an E6010 root welded uphill, then E7018 fill and cap, on a DC engine-driven welder with a remote control. Her first root shows icicles and too much penetration inside at the top of the pipe. On the next joint, near the open end of a long run of pipe, the arc keeps pulling to one side.

c3.title: Stainless parts and a cracked pump in Hayes
c3.text: Michelle is the lead welder at a food plant in Hayes, Clarendon. She must weld a strainer housing made of 3 mm grade 316L stainless steel; the plant has only MMAW machines. She must also repair a cast iron pump body with a 60 mm crack running in from a flange. The plant's maintenance store keeps one set of wire brushes and grinding discs, used on all metals.

c4.title: Built-up crane beams in Old Harbour
c4.text: A shop in Old Harbour, St Catherine, is building 8 m long I-beams for a crane runway from 12 mm flanges and a 10 mm web, with continuous fillet welds. On the first beam the team welded both top fillets end to end, then turned the beam over and welded the two bottom fillets. When it cooled, the beam had bowed 12 mm along its length. For the next beams, a team member suggests bolting the parts down hard in a heavy jig and welding everything at once.

c5.title: Inspection results on a warehouse frame in Santa Cruz
c5.text: Kerry-Ann is team leader for four welders on the steel frame of a warehouse in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. This week's visual inspection records show that welder W3 has undercut along most of his vertical welds, while his flat welds are good. A magnetic particle test has also found a crack at one beam-to-column weld, which is being ground out. The client's engineer wants the 25 mm thick column splices checked inside for lack of fusion, and does not want radiography on the busy site.

questions.q: Garfield has temperature crayons rated at 50 °C and at 250 °C. How should he use them on the flange joints?
o: The 50 °C mark must melt before welding; the 250 °C mark must not melt between runs
The 250 °C mark must melt before welding; the 50 °C mark must not melt between runs
Both marks must melt before the first run, to prove the preheat has soaked through
Neither crayon is needed, as the dew shows the steel is below the preheat
questions.why: A crayon mark melts when the steel reaches the crayon's rating. The 50 °C mark melting proves the minimum preheat; the 250 °C mark not melting proves the joint is below the maximum interpass temperature.

questions.q: What should be done about the dew on the steel before the splices are welded?
o: Wipe the joints with a clean, dry rag, then start the root run at once
Wait for the midday sun to dry them, then weld without preheat
Run the first pass fast and hot so the arc boils off the water
Warm each joint evenly until dry and up to the preheat, then check it
questions.why: Water on the joint puts hydrogen into the weld, and the WPS needs 50 °C anyway. Heat evenly across the joint area until it is dry and at least at the preheat, and check it with the crayon before welding.

questions.q: Between runs on a flange, a contact thermometer reads 290 °C on the plate. What should the welder do?
o: Carry on, as hotter steel means less risk of hydrogen cracking
Stop until the joint cools below 250 °C, then weld the next run
Cool the joint quickly with a wet rag so the work is not held up
Turn the current down by about 20% and carry on with the run
questions.why: The maximum interpass temperature protects the toughness of the weld and the heat-affected zone. Wait until the joint is back below 250 °C (but still above the 50 °C minimum); never quench it with water.

questions.q: Which part of the splices may Ricardo weld, given the positions on his qualification?
o: The bottom flange, as it is the same thickness as his test plate
The web, as vertical welding is close to horizontal welding
The top flange, as it is welded from above in the flat position
Any of them, as long as he follows the WPS for the splice
questions.why: His 1G and 2G test covers flat and horizontal work only. The web (vertical, 3G) and the bottom flange (overhead, 4G) need a welder qualified in those positions. Check the qualification record against each weld before giving it out.

questions.q: The weld symbol for the flange splices has a small flag where the arrow meets the reference line. What does the flag mean?
o: The weld is to be ground flush after welding
The weld goes all the way round the joint
The weld is made on the other side of the joint
The weld is made on site, not in the shop
questions.why: A flag at the junction of the arrow and the reference line marks a field weld. A circle at the same place means weld all round; a symbol above the line means the other side; a contour mark with G means grind.

questions.q: What change should Nordia make to cure the icicles and excess penetration at the top of the root?
o: Raise the current at the top so that the pool freezes more quickly
Lower the current a little there and travel slightly faster
Open the root gap wider so the metal has room to settle
Hold a longer arc at the top so the heat spreads out more
questions.why: By the time the root reaches the top, the pipe is hot and the pool is in the flat position, so it sags through. Use the remote to lower the current slightly, travel a little faster and keep the keyhole small.

questions.q: Which action is most likely to help with the arc pulling to one side near the open end of the pipe?
o: Move the work clamp, shorten the arc and angle the rod against the blow
Change the machine to AC but keep using the same E6010 electrodes
Turn the current right up so the arc is too strong to be pushed aside
Open up the root gap so the arc has more room to move about in the joint
questions.why: Arc blow on DC comes from magnetism in the pipe. Moving or wrapping the work lead, a shorter arc, angling against the blow and lower current all help. E6010 runs on DC only, so changing to AC would need an AC electrode and the WPS allowing it.

questions.q: Nordia's electrode runs out halfway up one side of the root. Before she restarts, what should she do to the end of the stopped run?
o: Leave it alone, as the new arc will melt it in
Hammer it flat so the new run sits on top of it
Chip it and grind it to a taper, then restart into it
Build a small tack beside it to start the new run from
questions.why: A crater left as it is gives a lump, a cold lap or a pinhole at the restart. Chipping it and grinding it to a taper lets the new run fuse smoothly into the old one, with the same keyhole on the inside.

questions.q: Where should Nordia start and finish each half of the uphill root?
o: Start just past 6 o'clock and finish just past 12 o'clock
Start at 12 o'clock and finish at 6 o'clock on each side
Start at 3 o'clock and weld down to 6 o'clock, then up
Start at 9 o'clock and weld right round to 9 o'clock again
questions.why: An uphill root starts at the bottom, just past 6 o'clock so the two halves overlap, and climbs each side to just past 12 o'clock. Starting at 12 o'clock and going down is the downhill method used on pipelines.

questions.q: Which electrode should Michelle use to weld the 316L strainer housing to itself?
o: E308L, as it is the usual electrode for stainless
E309L, as it is made for joining unlike steels
E7018, as it is a low-hydrogen electrode
E316L, to match the steel's molybdenum
questions.why: Grade 316L contains molybdenum for pitting resistance, so it is welded with the matching E316L. E308L has no molybdenum, E309L is for stainless to carbon steel, and E7018 is a carbon steel electrode.

questions.q: What should Michelle do about the shared wire brushes and grinding discs before working on the stainless housing?
o: Use them, as long as they are washed in solvent first
Use new brushes and discs kept only for stainless steel
Use them, then wash the housing down with water afterwards
Use the brushes, but cut and grind only with new discs
questions.why: Brushes and discs used on carbon steel leave iron particles in the stainless surface, which rust and spoil its corrosion resistance. Keep a separate set of stainless-only brushes, discs and clamps.

questions.q: What should Michelle do first, once she has found both ends of the crack in the pump body?
o: Weld a run along the crack to seal it before grinding
Heat the whole casting to a dull red to relieve its stress
Drill a small stop hole just beyond each end of the crack
Grind the crack out from the flange end only, then weld
questions.why: A small hole drilled just past each end stops the crack running further while it is ground out and welded. The crack is then ground out to sound metal before any welding.

questions.q: Why will Michelle weld the cast iron in runs of only about 30 mm, peening each one and letting it cool to hand-warm?
o: So the casting never gets hot enough for shrinkage stress to crack it
So the nickel weld metal becomes as hard as the cast iron around it
So that she uses less electrode, because nickel electrodes are costly
So that any gas in the casting has time to bubble out of the weld
questions.why: Cast iron cannot stretch, so a long, hot run shrinks and cracks it. Short runs, light peening while hot (which stretches the run) and cooling between runs keep the stress low; the nickel weld metal itself stays soft and ductile.

questions.q: Why did the first beam bow along its length?
o: The flanges were too thin for the size of fillet weld used
The shrinkage of the top fillets was not balanced by the bottom
The web was welded with too small an electrode for its thickness
The beam was turned over too soon, before the welds had set
questions.why: Both top fillets were finished before the bottom ones, so their shrinkage pulled the beam into a curve that the later welds could not pull back. Welding opposite fillets in turn, from the middle outwards, balances the pulls.

questions.q: What is the main risk of bolting each beam down hard in a heavy jig and welding everything without a planned sequence?
o: The beam will be pulled out of square as soon as it is unbolted
The jig will take the heat away and the welds will not fuse
Restraint holds it straight but locks in stress that can crack welds
The fillets will come out undersize because the parts cannot move at all
questions.why: A rigid jig stops movement, so the shrinkage turns into locked-in stress, which raises the risk of cracking and can still cause movement when the beam is released. Use clamps and jigs together with a balanced sequence.

questions.q: How should Kerry-Ann deal with the undercut on W3's vertical welds?
o: Watch him weld vertically, then show the cure and let him practise on scrap
Move him to flat welding only, as he cannot weld in the vertical position
Write a warning in the weld log and leave the welder to sort it out himself
Have the inspector grind and fill all of his undercut welds for him
questions.why: A fault in one position by one welder is a coaching matter. Watch him, check his settings, show the cure (correct current, shorter arc, pause at each edge), let him practise in the same position, and check his next welds.

questions.q: Once the crack has been ground out, how should Kerry-Ann confirm it has all gone before re-welding?
o: Look closely along the ground groove with a bright torch and a magnifier
Tap the groove with a hammer and listen for a dull sound
Test the ground area again with magnetic particles or dye penetrant
Weld a short test run in the groove and see whether it cracks
questions.why: A crack can be too fine to see once ground. Check the groove with the same kind of surface test that found it (magnetic particles on carbon steel, or dye penetrant) before it is re-welded to the repair procedure.

questions.q: Which test should be offered to the engineer for lack of fusion inside the 25 mm column splices?
o: Dye penetrant testing
Ultrasonic testing
Magnetic particle testing
A nick-break test
questions.why: Ultrasonic testing finds flat internal flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks in thick welds, with no radiation. Dye penetrant and magnetic particles find surface flaws only, and a nick-break test destroys the joint.

questions.q: A weld symbol shows a fillet triangle below the reference line, the number 8 to its left, and a circle where the arrow meets the line. What weld is needed?
o: An 8 mm fillet on the other side, along only 8 mm of the joint length
Fillet welds 8 mm long, spaced evenly round the joint
An 8 mm fillet weld on the arrow side, all round the joint
An 8 mm fillet on both sides, made on site as a field weld
questions.why: Below the line means arrow side; the number left of the triangle is the fillet size (leg length unless stated otherwise); the circle means weld all round. A flag, not a circle, would mean a site weld.

questions.q: Shawn must weld a pipe support inside a wet trench. Why should he use a machine fitted with a VRD?
o: It stops the arc from going out when the electrode gets damp
It lowers the welding current so that less heat reaches the pipe
It switches the machine off when water is felt near the leads
It keeps the open-circuit voltage low until the arc is struck
questions.why: Shocks usually come from the open-circuit voltage present whenever the machine is on. A voltage reduction device holds it at a low level until the electrode touches the work, which matters most in wet, cramped places.
